etymology: A rhyming catchphrase of the twentieth-century Word-of-Faith movement (E. W. Kenyon, Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland), sometimes mocked even by its own adherents as 'name it and claim it' or 'blab it and grab it.' The formula: name the thing desired — healing, wealth, a spouse, a parking space — and claim it as already yours by a 'word of faith,' on the premise that faith is a force that compels God to deliver.
biblical_def: Biblical prayer is petition offered to a sovereign God in submission to His will, never a technique for commanding Him. The pattern is fixed in Gethsemane, where the Son Himself prayed, 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39). The apostle frames all confident asking the same way: 'if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us' (1 John 5:14) — the confidence is real, but it is bounded by His will, not ours. So James rebukes the presumption that schedules God's hand: 'ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that' (James 4:15). Faith in Scripture is not a force we wield over God but trust we place in God; its posture is the empty open hand of a beggar, not the closed fist of a creditor. We name our requests; God, not our naming, decides.
webster_summary: A Word-of-Faith formula treating faith as a force that compels God to deliver what one 'claims'; rebutted by Gethsemane's 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39) and asking 'according to his will' (1 John 5:14).
webster_full: NAME IT AND CLAIM IT, slogan. A Word-of-Faith formula: name a desired thing and claim it as already granted by a 'word of faith.'
Source: the Word-of-Faith / Positive Confession movement (Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland); also mocked as 'blab it and grab it.'
Premise: faith is a spiritual force or law that, rightly applied, obligates God to deliver health and wealth.
Rebutted by Matt. 26:39 ('not as I will, but as thou wilt') and 1 John 5:14 (asking 'according to his will') — petition in submission, not command.
scriptures: Matthew 26:39
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
1 John 5:14
And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:
James 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
Job 42:2
I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
Psalm 115:3
But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.
James 4:3
Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.
corruption_summary: Word-of-Faith presumption turns prayer into a technique that commands God, treating faith as a force that obligates Him to deliver; Scripture answers that we ask 'according to his will' and bow, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt.'
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption inverts the creature and the Creator. In Scripture God is sovereign and man is a suppliant; 'name it and claim it' reverses the order, casting the believer as the one who decrees and God as the one obligated to perform. The Word-of-Faith teachers make this explicit: faith is reclassified as an impersonal 'force' or 'spiritual law' that operates by fixed principle, so that a confession spoken in sufficient faith must produce its object, and God Himself is bound by the law of faith He supposedly set in motion. This is not the God of the Bible, who 'hath done whatsoever he hath pleased' (Ps. 115:3) and whose counsel no man may withhold (Job 42:2). It is a domesticated deity, a vending machine that dispenses on the insertion of the right coin of confession. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the Word-of-Faith claim is named here to rebut it.

The doctrine also wounds the very souls it courts. When the named thing does not come — when the cancer is not healed, the bankruptcy not averted, the spouse not given — the system has only one explanation: the sufferer did not have enough faith, or spoke a stray word of doubt that 'cancelled' the claim. So affliction is compounded with guilt, and the sick are taught to blame themselves for a sovereignty that was never theirs to command. Scripture knows a holier sorrow: Paul prayed thrice that his thorn depart, and the answer was not a granted claim but a sufficient grace — 'My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor. 12:9). The apostle did not 'claim' his healing; he received his God.

The recovery is the prayer the Lord Himself prayed and taught. He taught us to ask, 'Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven' (Matt. 6:10), and He prayed in the garden, with the cup of wrath before Him, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39). That is the spine of all faithful prayer: bold to ask anything, humble to surrender everything, certain only that He 'doeth all things well' (Mark 7:37). The confidence of 1 John 5:14 is not the confidence of a man who has compelled God but of a child who trusts a Father — we ask 'according to his will,' and rest in it whether He grants or withholds.
roots_summary: A Word-of-Faith rhyme casting faith as a force that obligates God; Scripture makes prayer petition in submission — 'according to his will' (1 John 5:14), 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39).
roots_lines: English: a Word-of-Faith catchphrase (Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland); 'name' the desire, 'claim' it as granted by confession.
Greek (concept): proseuche, prayer as petition to God — in 1 John 5:14 bounded by 'according to his will' (kata to thelema autou).
Biblical posture: Matt. 26:39, the Son's 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' — the open hand of a suppliant, not the closed fist of a creditor.
usage: They told her to 'name it and claim it,' and when the healing did not come they told her she had not believed — affliction crowned with guilt.
The Son in the garden did not claim the cup away; He prayed 'not as I will, but as thou wilt,' and that is the spine of all true prayer.
Faith is not a force we wield over God but trust we place in God; we name the request and leave the granting to Him.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: Word-of-Faith presumption that commands God instead of beseeching Him; biblical prayer asks 'according to his will' and bows, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt.'

etymology: A motivational and Word-of-Faith catchphrase, popularized through prosperity preaching and self-help culture and now ubiquitous on social media: declare a desired outcome aloud as though speaking makes it so. The phrase consciously echoes the creation account — 'God said... and there was' — and transfers that creative power from God to the human tongue.
biblical_def: Creation by the word is the unique prerogative of God alone. 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth... And God said, Let there be light: and there was light' (Gen. 1:1-3); 'By the word of the LORD were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth... For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast' (Ps. 33:6,9). This fiat — calling 'those things which be not as though they were' (Rom. 4:17) — belongs to the Creator and to none of His creatures. Man's tongue has no such power. Its God-given function is to bless, to confess, to pray, to speak truth and edify (Eph. 4:29) — and it is held to fearful account, for 'by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned' (Matt. 12:37). The believer does not speak reality into being; he speaks to the God who alone called all things into being, and waits on Him.
webster_summary: A Word-of-Faith and self-help slogan applying God's unique creative fiat (Gen. 1) to the human tongue; but words are not creative power — only 'he spake, and it was done' (Ps. 33:9).
webster_full: SPEAK IT INTO EXISTENCE, slogan. To declare a desired outcome aloud on the premise that the declaration brings it to pass.
Sources: Word-of-Faith 'positive confession' and secular self-help / manifestation culture, now a social-media commonplace.
Premise: the spoken word carries creative or causal power to materialize what it names.
Rebutted by Gen. 1 and Ps. 33:6,9 — creation by the word is God's alone; the creature's tongue blesses, prays, and confesses, it does not create.
scriptures: Genesis 1:3
And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
Psalm 33:9
For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
Psalm 33:6
By the word of the LORD were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
Romans 4:17
(As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.
Matthew 12:37
For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.
Isaiah 55:11
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: The slogan steals God's unique creative prerogative — calling things that are not as though they were — and hands it to the human tongue; it is manifestation in Christian dress, and a quiet idolatry of the self.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a theft of divine prerogative. The creative word — 'he spake, and it was done' (Ps. 33:9) — is the signature of deity; to 'call those things which be not as though they were' is named in Romans 4:17 as the act of 'God, who quickeneth the dead.' To claim that power for one's own mouth is not a small exaggeration but a reach for the throne. In its Word-of-Faith form the claim is explicit: man is a 'little god' whose words carry the same creative force as God's, so that to speak a thing in faith is to bring it into being. In its secular form it is the law of attraction and 'manifestation,' the universe rearranging itself around one's declarations. The two are the same heresy in different vestments, and both forget that the creature speaks to the Creator, never as Him. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the manifestation claim is named here to rebut it.

The deeper sin is idolatry of the self. Manifestation makes the autonomous will the engine of reality and the spoken desire its lever; the self becomes a small sovereign, bending the world by decree. But Scripture knows only one sovereign mouth. It was the same lie at the first — 'ye shall be as gods' (Gen. 3:5) — that man might command rather than obey, create rather than receive. The Christianized version is more dangerous than the crude pagan kind precisely because it wears the language of Genesis and faith, baptizing a grasp at godhood in the vocabulary of devotion.

The recovery is to render the tongue to its true office and the creating to God. The believer's word does not make worlds; it confesses the One who did. Our speech is to be 'alway with grace, seasoned with salt' (Col. 4:6), used to bless and not curse, to pray and not presume, to edify and not boast (Eph. 4:29; James 3:9-10). And the only word that infallibly accomplishes what it names is His: 'it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please' (Isa. 55:11). We do not speak our future into existence; we entrust it to the God whose word upholds all things (Heb. 1:3).
roots_summary: A slogan transferring God's creative fiat (Gen. 1) to the human tongue; manifestation in Christian dress. Words do not create; God does — 'he spake, and it was done' (Ps. 33:9).
roots_lines: English: a Word-of-Faith and self-help phrase consciously echoing Genesis — 'God said... and there was.'
Hebrew (concept): the divine fiat of Gen. 1 ('and God said... and it was so') — creation by the word, God's prerogative alone.
Apostolic line: Rom. 4:17, God 'calleth those things which be not as though they were' — ascribed to God who quickens the dead, not to man.
usage: 'Speak it into existence' borrows the grammar of Genesis and forgets that only God said 'let there be' and there was.
Manifestation is the old lie 'ye shall be as gods' in a worship chorus; the creature speaks to the Creator, never as Him.
Our words bless, confess, and pray; the word that makes worlds and never returns void is His alone.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: Manifestation in Christian dress — it gives the human tongue God's creative fiat; words are not creative power, God is.

etymology: A therapeutic and self-help catchphrase of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, ubiquitous in talk-show and social-media culture: to 'live your truth' is to act in accordance with one's own felt, self-authored reality, on the premise that truth is private, personal, and self-determined — 'my truth' and 'your truth' may differ, and each is authoritative for the one who holds it.
biblical_def: Scripture knows no such thing as a private 'your truth'; it knows the truth, singular, objective, and grounded in the person of Christ. He declared, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6) — truth is not a feeling one authors but a Person one bows to. God's 'word is truth' (John 17:17), and His judgments are 'true and righteous altogether' (Ps. 19:9). Against the self-authored path Scripture sets a sober warning: 'There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death' (Prov. 14:12) — the very thing the slogan commends (following the way that seems right to oneself) is the thing Scripture flags as deadly. Liberty comes not from living one's own truth but from submitting to His: 'ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free' (John 8:32). Truth is discovered and obeyed, never invented.
webster_summary: A therapeutic slogan asserting private, self-authored 'truth'; but Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and the way that merely seems right to a man ends in death (Prov. 14:12).
webster_full: LIVE YOUR TRUTH, slogan. To act on one's own felt, self-determined reality as if it were authoritative truth.
Cultural source: therapeutic and self-help culture; the postmodern premise that truth is personal and plural ('my truth' / 'your truth').
Structurally it relocates truth from objective reality to private feeling, making the self its own final authority.
Rebutted by John 14:6 (Christ is the truth), John 17:17 (God's word is truth), and Prov. 14:12 (the self-chosen way ends in death).
scriptures: John 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Proverbs 14:12
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
John 17:17
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
John 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Judges 21:25
In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Isaiah 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
corruption_summary: The slogan privatizes truth into 'my truth' and 'your truth,' enthroning the self as its own authority; but Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and the way that seems right to a man ends in death (Prov. 14:12).
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is at the root: it relocates truth from God to the self. Biblically, truth is what corresponds to reality as God has made and revealed it; it is one, because He is one, and it stands whether any man believes it or not. 'Live your truth' denies this, dividing truth into as many private truths as there are persons and making each one's feelings the final court. This is postmodernism's central claim — that there is no truth above the knower, only perspectives — dressed in the warm language of authenticity. But a 'truth' that is merely mine is not truth at all; it is preference wearing truth's crown. Scripture's verdict on the era when 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes' (Judg. 21:25) is not admiration but lament: it was Israel's anarchy and ruin. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the 'your truth' framing is named here to rebut it.

The slogan is also cruel beneath its kindness. It flatters a man that whatever seems right to him is right for him, and Scripture answers with a warning aimed at exactly that flattery: 'There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death' (Prov. 14:12). To tell a soul to follow the way that seems right to it, with no truth above it to correct it, is to send it confidently down the road Proverbs names deadly. And it ends, as Isaiah saw, in the calling of 'evil good, and good evil' (Isa. 5:20) — for once 'my truth' is sovereign, there is no fixed light by which darkness can still be called dark.

The recovery is the freedom of submission to the one Truth. Jesus did not say 'find your truth' but 'I am... the truth' (John 14:6), and He bound liberty to that truth received and obeyed: 'ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free' (John 8:32). Real freedom is not the autonomy to author reality but release from the bondage of self-deception by the Word that is truth (John 17:17). The Christian does not live his truth; he dies to it, and lives by Christ's — and there, not in the prison of the self, he is finally free.
roots_summary: A therapeutic slogan privatizing truth into the self's authority; Scripture answers that Christ is the truth (John 14:6) and the self-chosen way ends in death (Prov. 14:12). Truth is obeyed, not invented.
roots_lines: English: a self-help / talk-show catchphrase resting on the postmodern premise of plural, personal 'truths.'
Greek: aletheia, truth as what is unconcealed and real — in John 14:6 identified with the Person of Christ, not a private feeling.
Biblical warning: Prov. 14:12, the way that 'seemeth right unto a man' ends in death — the very self-led path the slogan commends.
usage: 'Live your truth' divides truth into as many truths as there are people, but Christ said 'I am the truth,' not 'find yours.'
The slogan flatters the way that seems right to a man — the very road Proverbs calls the way of death.
Freedom is not authoring reality but bowing to the One who is truth; we die to our truth to live by His.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: There is no private 'your truth'; Christ is the truth, and the way that seems right to a man ends in death.

etymology: A slogan made famous by Rob Bell's 2011 book Love Wins: A Book About Heaven, Hell, and the Fate of Every Person Who Ever Lived, which questioned the doctrine of eternal conscious punishment, and afterward a banner of the same-sex-marriage campaigns. In both uses 'love wins' asserts that divine love must finally override judgment, wrath, and any unwelcome boundary — love as a sentiment that triumphs by abolishing holiness.
biblical_def: Love does indeed triumph in the gospel — but it triumphs at the cross, where it is precisely holiness and justice satisfied, not abolished. The supreme definition of love is propitiatory: 'Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins' (1 John 4:10). And the cross is where God's love and God's justice meet without compromise: God set forth Christ 'to be a propitiation through faith in his blood... to declare his righteousness... that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus' (Rom. 3:25-26). There love 'wins' — not by waving away sin but by bearing its full wrath in the Son, so that mercy and justice kiss (Ps. 85:10). A 'love' that wins by emptying the cross of wrath has not exalted love; it has destroyed it, for the measure of that love is the wrath it absorbed. 'Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends' (John 15:13).
webster_summary: Rob Bell's slogan collapsing holiness and justice into sentiment, so love 'wins' by abolishing wrath; but love wins at the cross, where wrath is satisfied (Rom. 3:25-26; 1 John 4:10).
webster_full: LOVE WINS, slogan. The claim that divine love must finally override judgment, hell, and any boundary love finds unwelcome.
Sources: Rob Bell, Love Wins (2011), questioning eternal punishment; later a same-sex-marriage campaign banner.
Premise: love and wrath are rivals, so love's victory means the abolition of wrath and the dissolving of boundaries.
Rebutted by 1 John 4:10 (love defined as propitiation) and Rom. 3:25-26 (the cross is love AND justice satisfied, not justice waived).
scriptures: 1 John 4:10
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
Romans 3:25-26

Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
John 15:13
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Psalm 85:10
Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
Romans 5:8
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
John 3:36
He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.
corruption_summary: The slogan makes love the rival of wrath and declares love the winner by abolishing judgment; but love wins precisely at the cross, where God's justice is satisfied so that He is 'just, and the justifier' (Rom. 3:26).
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption sets love and justice at war and then crowns a love that has conquered holiness — which is no biblical love at all. In Scripture the attributes of God are not rivals to be ranked; they are one in His simple, undivided being, so that His love is holy love and His mercy is just mercy. 'Love wins,' in Bell's deployment, severs love from justice and asks us to choose love — with the result that hell is emptied, wrath is denied, and the boundaries of the moral law dissolve as obstacles to a sentimental affection. But a love that overrides justice is not the love of the cross; it is mere indulgence, and it makes the death of Christ unnecessary. If love could simply win by waiving the penalty, then Calvary was a ghastly mistake, and the Father 'spared not his own Son' (Rom. 8:32) for nothing. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan is named here to rebut it.

The same flattening underwrites the later 'love wins' of the marriage campaigns: love, redefined as the affirmation of any desire that calls itself love, is declared the victor over the 'unloving' boundaries of God's creational order. But 1 Corinthians 13 already settled that love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (13:6). A 'win' for love that consists in rejoicing over what God forbids is a defeat dressed as a triumph. Real love never wins by lying about the good of the beloved; it wins by telling, and bearing, the truth.

The recovery is to behold where love actually wins. It wins at Golgotha, where 'mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other' (Ps. 85:10) — where the wrath that justice required was poured out on the Substitute so that the love that mercy intended could flow to the guilty. There God is shown 'just, and the justifier of him which believeth' (Rom. 3:26): not justice abandoned for love, but justice and love magnified together. Love does win — but its victory is measured by the wrath it bore, not by the wrath it denied. Deny the wrath and you have not enlarged the love; you have abolished it.
roots_summary: A Rob Bell slogan ranking love above justice and emptying hell; Scripture shows love winning at the cross, where wrath is satisfied and God is 'just, and the justifier' (Rom. 3:26; 1 John 4:10).
roots_lines: English: the title of Rob Bell's 2011 book questioning eternal punishment; later a same-sex-marriage banner.
Greek: hilasmos, propitiation — love defined in 1 John 4:10 as the sending of the Son to bear wrath, not to waive it.
The cross: Rom. 3:25-26, God 'just, and the justifier' — love wins by justice satisfied, never by justice abolished.
usage: 'Love wins' by emptying hell makes the cross a needless cruelty; love won there by bearing the wrath, not by denying it.
Mercy and truth met at Golgotha; a love that wins by overriding justice is indulgence, not the love of God.
The measure of the love that wins is the wrath it absorbed — deny the wrath and you have abolished the love.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: It crowns a love that abolishes wrath; but love wins at the cross, where wrath is satisfied and God is 'just, and the justifier.'

etymology: A devotional catchphrase popularized through the Keswick 'higher life' and Victorious Christian Life movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and widely adopted in recovery and self-help settings. The formula: stop striving (let go) and let God do the work (let God), on the premise that human effort is the enemy of grace and that surrender means passivity.
biblical_def: Scripture commands a dependence that is anything but passive — an active, strenuous obedience that draws its very strength from the God who works in us. The decisive text holds both halves together in a single breath: 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure' (Phil. 2:12-13). The believer truly works — 'work out' — precisely because God works in him; divine working does not cancel human effort but empowers it. So Paul says of his own labor, 'I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me' (1 Cor. 15:10) — full effort, wholly of grace. The Christian life is a fight (1 Tim. 6:12), a race (Heb. 12:1), a putting to death of the deeds of the body 'through the Spirit' (Rom. 8:13). Trust is not the surrender of effort but its source; we rest in God by working hard in His strength, not by going limp.
webster_summary: A 'higher life' slogan mistaking passivity for trust; but Scripture commands active dependence — 'work out your own salvation... for it is God which worketh in you' (Phil. 2:12-13).
webster_full: LET GO AND LET GOD, slogan. To cease striving and leave the work to God, treating surrender as passivity.
Source: the Keswick / 'higher life' / Victorious Christian Life tradition; widely adopted in recovery and self-help.
Half-true: it rightly rejects self-reliant striving and rightly commends dependence on God.
Half-false where it makes effort the enemy of grace; Phil. 2:12-13 and 1 Cor. 15:10 command full effort empowered by grace, not passivity.
scriptures: Philippians 2:12-13

Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
1 Corinthians 15:10
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Colossians 1:29
Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.
1 Timothy 6:12
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Romans 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Philippians 4:13
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
corruption_summary: A quietism that mistakes passivity for trust and makes effort the enemy of grace; Scripture binds the two — 'work out your own salvation... for it is God which worketh in you' (Phil. 2:12-13).
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the error is an old devotional one — a quietism that reads surrender as going limp. The slogan contains a real and precious truth: we cannot sanctify ourselves by raw willpower, and the self-reliant striving of the flesh is bankrupt. So far it is right, and it rightly rebukes the proud activism that leaves God out. But it overshoots into a false antithesis — that human effort and divine grace are rivals, so that the more I do, the less God does, and the truest faith is therefore to stop doing and 'let God.' Scripture refuses that antithesis flatly. Paul 'laboured more abundantly than they all,' and in the same sentence ascribes every ounce of it to grace: 'yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me' (1 Cor. 15:10). Grace is not the alternative to effort; grace is what makes the effort possible and fruitful.

The practical damage of the quietist reading is real. It can teach the struggling believer that the mark of faith is to cease the fight against sin and simply 'rest,' when Scripture commands him to 'mortify the deeds of the body' (Rom. 8:13) and to 'fight the good fight of faith' (1 Tim. 6:12). It can baptize spiritual sloth as surrender, leaving besetting sins unmortified under the pretext of trusting God to do what He has plainly commanded the believer to do in His strength. The passive Christian waiting to be zapped into holiness while neglecting the means of grace has not exercised great faith; he has misunderstood it.

The recovery is the active dependence of Philippians 2:12-13: 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you.' The conjunction is everything — for, not so. Because God works in you, therefore work; the indwelling power is the ground of the strenuous obedience, not a substitute for it. Paul described his own ministry exactly so: 'I labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily' (Col. 1:29). The believer does not let go of effort and wait; he throws himself into the fight, and finds the strength he spends is supplied by Another (Phil. 4:13).
roots_summary: A 'higher life' quietism that mistakes passivity for trust; Scripture commands active dependence — 'work out your own salvation... for it is God which worketh in you' (Phil. 2:12-13). We labor from God's working, not instead of it.
roots_lines: English: a Keswick / 'higher life' devotional slogan, later common in recovery and self-help settings.
Biblical correction: Phil. 2:12-13 binds working out and God's working in — the conjunction is 'for,' not 'instead.'
Pattern of grace: 1 Cor. 15:10, 'I laboured... yet not I, but the grace of God' — full effort, wholly of grace, never passivity.
usage: He 'let go and let God' of a sin God told him to mortify — calling sloth surrender does not make it faith.
Paul labored more than them all and called it all grace; effort and grace are not rivals but partners.
We do not go limp and wait to be zapped holy; we fight the good fight in the strength God supplies.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A real truth (we cannot self-sanctify) bent into passivity; Scripture commands active dependence — work, for it is God who works in you.

etymology: A condolence formula of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries — 'you are in our thoughts and prayers' — once a sincere expression of sympathy and intercession, now so worn by repetition (especially in public statements after tragedies) that it is widely heard as empty boilerplate and openly mocked as a substitute for action.
biblical_def: Real prayer for the afflicted is a holy and powerful thing, and Scripture commands it: 'pray one for another... The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much' (James 5:16); 'is any among you afflicted? let him pray' (James 5:13); 'Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ' (Gal. 6:2). But Scripture is equally severe against words of sympathy that cost nothing and do nothing. James himself draws the line: 'If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?' (James 2:15-16). And John: 'let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth' (1 John 3:18). Biblical intercession, then, is fervent, not formulaic, and where it can act it acts — prayer and the open hand together, never the warm word alone.
webster_summary: Once a sincere condolence of sympathy and intercession, now often hollow boilerplate; recover real, fervent prayer that also acts — not 'be ye warmed and filled' with empty hands (James 2:16; 5:16).
webster_full: THOUGHTS AND PRAYERS, slogan. A condolence formula offering sympathy and intercession to the suffering.
Once sincere; now widely heard as empty boilerplate, especially in public statements after tragedies, and mocked as a dodge from action.
The phrase is not wrong; the hollowing of it is — a costless word offered where deeds are also owed.
Measured by James 2:15-16 ('be ye warmed and filled... what doth it profit?') and James 5:16 ('the effectual fervent prayer... availeth much').
scriptures: James 2:15-16

If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?
James 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
1 John 3:18
My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
James 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Matthew 6:7
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
corruption_summary: A once-sincere phrase is hollowed into performative sympathy — a costless word where deeds are also owed; recover real, fervent intercession that prays and acts (James 2:16; 5:16; 1 John 3:18).
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not heresy but hollowing — a true thing emptied by rote until it becomes the very 'be ye warmed and filled' that James condemns (James 2:16). The phrase began as a genuine pledge: I will hold you in my mind and lift you before God. But repeated as automatic public boilerplate, detached from any actual fervent prayer and from any deed where deeds are possible, it curdles into a gesture — a way to appear caring while remaining uninvolved. James 2:15-16 names the failure exactly: warm words to the naked and hungry, with no bread in the hand, 'what doth it profit?' The world's mockery of 'thoughts and prayers,' though often aimed unfairly at prayer itself, has landed on a real fault — the divorce of sympathetic speech from sacrificial action.

Two abuses must be distinguished from the genuine grace. The first is the empty word that never becomes prayer at all: the speaker says 'praying for you' and never does. That is a small lie, and 'let us not love in word, neither in tongue' (1 John 3:18) forbids it. The second is real prayer offered as a substitute for an action that God has put within the speaker's power — praying for the hungry man one could feed, the lonely one could visit, the wronged one could defend. Prayer is never an excuse to leave undone what love and ability make possible; 'to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin' (James 4:17).

The recovery is to make the phrase mean again what it says, and to add the hand to the heart. Where I can only pray — for the distant, the dying, the matters beyond my reach — let me pray in earnest, for 'the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much' (James 5:16), and intercession is no small thing but a real laying hold of God. And where I can also act, let prayer drive me to act: to bear the burden (Gal. 6:2), to give the bread, to be myself part of the answer I ask God to send. Then 'thoughts and prayers' is no slogan but the truth — love in deed and in truth (1 John 3:18).
roots_summary: A sincere condolence hollowed by rote into performative sympathy; recover fervent intercession joined to action — not warm words with empty hands (James 2:16), but love 'in deed and in truth' (1 John 3:18).
roots_lines: English: a modern condolence formula, once sincere, now often empty boilerplate mocked as a dodge from action.
Apostolic standard: James 2:15-16, 'be ye warmed and filled' with no bread — sympathy without deeds 'profiteth' nothing.
Power of real prayer: James 5:16, 'the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much' — intercession is no empty gesture.
usage: 'Thoughts and prayers' meant something once; rote and unaccompanied by deeds, it becomes the 'be ye warmed and filled' James condemns.
Pray in earnest for what is beyond your reach, and act on what is within it — prayer is never a hiding place from love.
Where I can feed the hungry man, my prayer for him is no substitute for the bread he needs today.

etymology: A revivalist and youth-ministry catchphrase of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries describing a state of intense emotional zeal — to be 'on fire for God' is to feel fervent, excited, and visibly passionate. The fire imagery draws loosely on Pentecost and on Jeremiah's 'fire shut up in my bones,' but in usage it has narrowed to a metric of emotional heat.
biblical_def: Scripture commends real spiritual fervor — 'fervent in spirit; serving the Lord' (Rom. 12:11) — but it ties that warmth to knowledge and proves it by endurance, not by the height of a feeling. Paul's lament over Israel is the standing caution: 'they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2). Zeal untethered from truth is not a virtue but a danger; it burned in Saul of Tarsus while he persecuted the church (Phil. 3:6). Genuine love for God is therefore not measured by emotional intensity but by obedience over time: 'If ye love me, keep my commandments' (John 14:15); 'he that endureth to the end shall be saved' (Matt. 24:13). The faithful servant is praised not for fervor but for being 'faithful over a few things' across the long haul (Matt. 25:21). The fire Scripture wants is a steady hearth that warms a household for decades, not a flare that lights the sky and is gone by morning.
webster_summary: A revivalist metric of emotional zeal that burns hot and fades; recover steady, knowledgeable faithfulness — 'zeal... but not according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2), the slow obedience of a lifetime.
webster_full: ON FIRE FOR GOD, slogan. A state of intense, visible emotional zeal for God, prized as the mark of true devotion.
Source: revivalist and youth-ministry culture; fire imagery loosely from Pentecost and Jer. 20:9.
Half-true: Scripture commends real fervor, 'fervent in spirit; serving the Lord' (Rom. 12:11).
Cautioned: zeal must be 'according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2) and is proved by endurance (Matt. 24:13), not by emotional heat that fades.

For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Romans 12:11
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
John 14:15
If ye love me, keep my commandments.
Matthew 24:13
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Galatians 4:18
But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you.
Luke 8:13
They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.
corruption_summary: An emotional-zeal metric that prizes heat over knowledge and endurance; recover steady, knowledgeable faithfulness — zeal 'according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2) proved by the slow obedience of a lifetime.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is a sub-biblical measure of devotion — the equating of love for God with emotional temperature. The slogan is not false, for Scripture does command fervor: 'fervent in spirit; serving the Lord' (Rom. 12:11), and zeal 'in a good thing' is good (Gal. 4:18). But 'on fire for God' as commonly used measures the wrong thing. It gauges the intensity of a feeling at a moment — the goosebumps at the conference, the tears at the worship set — and treats that heat as the proof of spiritual life. Scripture's own warnings cut straight across this. Israel's zeal was real and hot, yet ruinous, because it was 'not according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2); the seed on the rock received the word 'with joy' and great fervor, and withered for lack of root (Luke 8:13). Heat is not the test; truth and root are.

The practical harm is two-fold. First, it produces the flare-and-fade pattern: young believers are stirred to white-hot enthusiasm, taught to chase the next emotional peak, and then crash into disillusionment when the feeling inevitably cools — mistaking the cooling of an emotion for the loss of their faith. Second, it quietly despises the very thing Scripture prizes: the unspectacular, knowledgeable, persevering obedience of ordinary saints who keep the commandments (John 14:15), raise their children, attend the means of grace, and endure to the end (Matt. 24:13) without ever feeling 'on fire.' That steady faithfulness is treated as lukewarm when it is in fact the mature article.

The recovery is to trade the flare for the hearth. Real zeal is to be 'zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present' (Gal. 4:18) — always, the steady constancy that outlasts the emotional weather. Let fervor be welcomed where God grants it, but let it be fervor 'according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2), rooted in the Word, expressed in obedience, and proved not by how high it leaps in an hour but by how long it burns across a life. The Lord crowns the servant 'faithful over a few things' (Matt. 25:21), and the fire He prizes is the one still warming the house at the end of the road.
roots_summary: A revivalist metric of emotional heat that flares and fades; recover steady, knowledgeable faithfulness — zeal 'according to knowledge' (Rom. 10:2), proved by enduring obedience (Matt. 24:13), not by feeling.
roots_lines: English: a revivalist / youth-ministry phrase; fire imagery loosely from Pentecost and Jer. 20:9, narrowed to emotional heat.
Biblical caution: Rom. 10:2, Israel's 'zeal of God, but not according to knowledge' — fervor untethered from truth is a danger.
True measure: John 14:15 and Matt. 24:13 — love proved by keeping the commandments and enduring to the end, not by heat.
usage: He was 'on fire for God' at the conference and cold by Lent, mistaking the cooling of a feeling for the loss of his faith.
Israel's zeal was hot and ruinous because it was not according to knowledge; heat is not the test, truth and root are.
The fire God prizes is the hearth that warms a household for decades, not the flare gone by morning.

etymology: A common evangelical idiom — 'God laid it on my heart' — used to report a subjective inward impression, prompting, or burden as though it carried divine authority. The phrase has no direct biblical wording; it grows out of charismatic and revivalist habits of speech in which inward feelings are narrated as direct messages from God.
biblical_def: God does providentially incline and move the hearts of His people (Prov. 21:1; Neh. 2:12, where God 'put' a purpose in Nehemiah's heart), and there is nothing false in a believer's sense of burden or leading. But Scripture never lets a subjective impression stand as its own authority; every such prompting must be brought to the bar of the written Word, which alone binds the conscience. 'Prove all things; hold fast that which is good' (1 Thess. 5:21). 'Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God' (1 John 4:1). And the touchstone is fixed: 'To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them' (Isa. 8:20). The closed canon is the only sure word; an impression may be from God, from the flesh, or from the deceitful heart that is 'deceitful above all things' (Jer. 17:9). Therefore feelings are to be tested by Scripture, never Scripture by feelings; what aligns with the Word is heeded, what contradicts it is rejected, whatever the strength of the inward sense.
webster_summary: An evangelical idiom treating a subjective impression as divine authority; but impressions must be tested by the written Word (1 Thess. 5:21; Isa. 8:20), which alone binds the conscience.
webster_full: LAID IT ON MY HEART, slogan. To report an inward impression or burden as a direct message from God.
No biblical wording; grows from charismatic/revivalist habits of narrating feelings as divine communication.
Half-true: God does incline His people's hearts (Neh. 2:12; Prov. 21:1), and burdens may be genuine.
Cautioned: 1 Thess. 5:21 ('prove all things'), 1 John 4:1 ('try the spirits'), and Isa. 8:20 ('to the law and to the testimony') — impressions are tested by the Word, never the Word by impressions.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 5:21
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Isaiah 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
1 John 4:1

Jeremiah 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Proverbs 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Acts 17:11
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: The idiom elevates a subjective impression to the authority of a divine word; but the deceitful heart (Jer. 17:9) must be tested by Scripture (1 Thess. 5:21; Isa. 8:20), which alone binds the conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is a misplaced authority — the treating of a private feeling as an unquestionable 'word from God.' The phrase is not inherently wrong; God truly does move the hearts of His people (Prov. 21:1), and to feel a burden for a person or a task is no sin. The corruption enters when 'God laid it on my heart' is wielded as a conversation-ending claim of divine sanction, immune to question, correction, or the test of Scripture — as though to challenge the impression were to challenge God Himself. That move smuggles a private revelation into the place that belongs to the closed canon alone, and it can be used to justify nearly anything: a rash decision, a wounding word, a marriage, a move, a doctrine — all shielded from examination because 'the Lord told me.' But Jeremiah warns that 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jer. 17:9); the very organ on which the thing is supposedly 'laid' is the one Scripture flags as least trustworthy.

The biblical safeguard is the testing of every impression by the written Word. 'Prove all things' (1 Thess. 5:21); 'try the spirits' (1 John 4:1); and the unbending rule, 'to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them' (Isa. 8:20). An inward prompting is not authoritative because it is inward and felt strongly; it is to be weighed, and only what accords with Scripture is to be heeded. The Bereans are praised precisely for this — they did not accept even an apostle's preaching on the strength of feeling but 'searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so' (Acts 17:11). How much more must a private impression submit to that same searching.

The recovery is to keep the conscience bound to Scripture alone and impressions firmly subordinate to it. A burden may rightly prompt prayer, counsel, and action — but it possesses no authority of its own; it does not bind another, and it does not bind even the one who feels it apart from the Word. Where an impression aligns with Scripture, follow the Scripture (the impression added nothing); where it contradicts Scripture, reject it however vivid; where Scripture is silent, walk by wisdom, counsel, and providence (Prov. 11:14), not by treating a feeling as a verse. 'God laid it on my heart' is safe only when it means 'and I have tested it by His Word.'
roots_summary: An idiom that makes a subjective impression a divine word; Scripture subordinates every prompting to the written Word — 'prove all things' (1 Thess. 5:21), 'to the law and to the testimony' (Isa. 8:20), which alone binds the conscience.
roots_lines: English: an evangelical idiom narrating an inward impression as a direct message from God; no biblical wording.
Biblical caution: Jer. 17:9, 'the heart is deceitful above all things' — the felt impression is no self-authenticating word.
The test: Isa. 8:20 and 1 Thess. 5:21 — every prompting is proved by the written Word, which alone binds the conscience.
usage: He ended every argument with 'God laid it on my heart,' as though a feeling were a verse no one might question.
The heart is deceitful above all things — the very place a thing is 'laid' is the one Scripture trusts least.
An impression that agrees with Scripture adds nothing; one that contradicts it is rejected, however strong the feeling.

verdict.line: A subjective impression dressed as divine authority; impressions must be tested by the written Word, which alone binds the conscience.

etymology: A prayer-meeting idiom — 'we ask a hedge of protection around them' — drawn directly from Satan's complaint about Job: 'Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?' (Job 1:10). The image is a thorny boundary God sets about His people to keep harm out; the phrase is biblical in source, but has become a rote formula through sheer repetition.
biblical_def: The image is genuinely scriptural and rich. In Job, the accuser concedes that God has 'made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side' (Job 1:10) — a divine protection so real that Satan could not touch Job until God lifted it. The same protecting care runs through Scripture: 'The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them' (Ps. 34:7); 'As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people' (Ps. 125:2); 'thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy' (Ps. 61:3). To pray a hedge of protection, then, is to ask God to be about His people as He was about Job — sound doctrine and a fitting prayer. The only caution is the Job context itself: the hedge is God's to raise and to lower for His own wise purposes, so the prayer must be offered in submission, trusting His protection and His permitted afflictions alike.
webster_summary: A biblical image (Job 1:10) of God's protecting boundary about His people; sound imagery worn merely rote by overuse — a gentle call to mean it, and to pray it in submission to the God who raises and lowers the hedge.
webster_full: HEDGE OF PROTECTION, noun phrase. God's protecting boundary set about His people to keep harm out.
Source: Job 1:10, Satan's concession that God had 'made an hedge about' Job and all he had.
Sound imagery, echoed in Ps. 34:7, Ps. 125:2, Ps. 61:3 — the LORD round about them that fear Him.
Caution is only rote-ness: the phrase is often repeated mechanically; and Job's context shows the hedge is God's to raise and lower in His wisdom.
scriptures: Job 1:10
Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
Psalm 34:7
The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
Psalm 125:2
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Psalm 5:12

Zechariah 2:5
For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.
corruption_summary: Drawn from Job 1:10, the image is sound and the prayer fitting; the only fault is rote-ness — a phrase repeated mechanically. A gentle call to mean it, and to pray it in submission to the God who both raises and lowers the hedge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and indeed faces no real corruption at all — the phrase is biblical in source and sound in sense. The image comes straight from Scripture: Satan, in Job 1:10, is forced to admit that God had 'made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side.' That hedge was a true and effective protection; the accuser could not lay a finger on Job until God Himself drew it back. To ask the same protecting boundary for the saints — that the Lord would be 'round about his people' as the mountains are round about Jerusalem (Ps. 125:2) — is faithful prayer in faithful words. The only thing to examine is not the doctrine but the heart of the one praying: whether the phrase has gone limp through endless repetition into a thoughtless filler reached for at every prayer meeting, the lips moving while the mind sleeps.

There is a second, gentle caution drawn from the very passage the phrase quotes. In Job, the hedge is God's hedge — His to set and His to lift — and He lowered it, for holy reasons Job could not see, that His servant might be tried and in the end more blessed (Job 1:12; 42:12). So the prayer for a hedge must never harden into a demand that God shield His people from all affliction, as though protection were owed and suffering a sign of failed faith. The same God who hedges may, in wisdom, permit the storm; 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' (Job 2:10). The prayer is offered, like all prayer, in submission to His will (Matt. 26:39), trusting both the hedge He raises and the trials He permits.

The recovery, then, is simply to mean it. Let 'a hedge of protection' be prayed with the weight Job's account gives it — a real plea to a real God who really compasses the righteous 'with favour... as with a shield' (Ps. 5:12) and is 'a wall of fire round about' His city (Zech. 2:5). Pray it thoughtfully, not by rote; pray it in submission, not as a demand; and let the familiar words carry the living faith they were meant to carry. A worn coin is still gold; the cure for a rote prayer is not to discard it but to pray it from the heart.
roots_summary: A biblical image (Job 1:10) of God's protecting boundary about His people; sound and fitting, faulted only by rote repetition. Mean it, and pray it in submission to the God who both raises and lowers the hedge.
roots_lines: English: a prayer-meeting idiom drawn directly from Job 1:10, Satan's concession of the 'hedge about' Job.
Biblical echoes: Ps. 34:7, Ps. 125:2, Zech. 2:5 — the LORD encamped round about, a wall of fire, mountains about Jerusalem.
The caution from Job: the hedge is God's to raise and lower (Job 1:12) — pray it in submission, not as a demand against all affliction.

God hedged Job and then, for holy reasons, lowered the hedge — pray for protection in submission, not as a demand.
A worn coin is still gold; the cure for a rote prayer is not to drop it but to mean it.

verdict.line: Sound biblical imagery from Job 1:10, merely worn rote by overuse — a gentle call to mean it and pray it in submission.

etymology: An idiom drawn from Gideon's sign in Judges 6: laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asking God to make it wet while the ground stayed dry, then dry while the ground stayed wet, as confirmation of His word. 'Putting out a fleece' has come to mean devising a sign or test and asking God to perform it to confirm guidance — treating Gideon's act as a method to imitate.
biblical_def: Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40) was not a model of faith offered for imitation but an instance of weak faith graciously accommodated. God had already given Gideon His clear word — 'Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man' (Judg. 6:16) — confirmed by an angel, a sign of fire from the rock, and more. The fleece was Gideon asking for still more proof of a promise already plainly given, and even there he confessed his fear of presumption: 'Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once' (Judg. 6:39). God in mercy stooped to his weakness, but the episode commends God's patience, not Gideon's method. Scripture's settled way of guidance is otherwise: God leads by His revealed Word (Ps. 119:105), by wisdom and counsel (Prov. 11:14), and by His providence ordering circumstances (Prov. 16:9) — not by signs we devise and demand. Indeed the Lord rebukes sign-seeking: 'An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign' (Matt. 12:39), and 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God' (Matt. 4:7).
webster_summary: Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40) was unbelief graciously accommodated, not a guidance method to imitate; God guides by His Word, wisdom, and providence, not by signs we devise and demand (Matt. 12:39; 4:7).
webster_full: PUTTING OUT A FLEECE, slogan. Devising a sign or test and asking God to perform it to confirm guidance.
Source: Gideon's fleece in Judg. 6:36-40 — wet fleece on dry ground, then dry fleece on wet ground.
Misread as a model: Gideon was asking more proof of a promise God had already plainly given (Judg. 6:16), and feared his own presumption (6:39).
Corrected by Matt. 12:39 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign') and Matt. 4:7 ('thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God').
scriptures: Judges 6:39

And Gideon said unto God, Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once: let me prove, I pray thee, but this once with the fleece; let it now be dry only upon the fleece, and upon all the ground let there be dew.
Judges 6:16
And the LORD said unto him, Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man.
Matthew 12:39
But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas:
Matthew 4:7
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
Psalm 119:105

corruption_summary: Gideon's fleece is misread as a guidance method to copy; it was weak faith graciously accommodated, not a model. God guides by His Word, wisdom, and providence — not by signs we devise and demand (Matt. 12:39; 4:7).
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the error is a misreading of a narrative — turning Gideon's fleece into a technique. The account is told not to give a guidance method but to show God's astonishing patience with a fearful man. The LORD had already spoken with total clarity: 'Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man' (Judg. 6:16). He had sent an angel, consumed an offering with fire from a rock (6:21), and answered Gideon's first request. The fleece was therefore not faith reaching for guidance but unbelief reaching for one more proof of a promise already given — and Gideon knew it, pleading 'let not thine anger be hot against me' (6:39), conscious that he stood near to tempting God. To read his trembling as a pattern for the believer is to commend the weakness the narrative gently exposes, not the faith it records elsewhere (Heb. 11:32).

The practical danger is that 'putting out a fleece' substitutes a self-devised sign for the means of guidance God has actually appointed. The believer who refuses to act until a parking space opens, a phone rings by a certain hour, or some arbitrary token appears has not exercised faith; he has shifted the weight of decision onto a sign of his own making and called it trusting God. Worse, he edges toward the very thing the Lord forbade in the wilderness: 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God' (Matt. 4:7). And he stands under the rebuke of Matthew 12:39 — for it is 'an evil and adulterous generation' that 'seeketh after a sign.' Christian guidance is not the manipulation of providence by tests but trust in the God who orders providence.

The recovery is to seek guidance the way Scripture actually appoints. 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Ps. 119:105): the Word is the first and surest guide, settling most questions of duty before any 'leading' is sought. Where the Word does not speak directly, God guides by sanctified wisdom and godly counsel — 'in the multitude of counsellors there is safety' (Prov. 11:14) — and by His providence, for 'a man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps' (Prov. 16:9). The believer trusts in the LORD with all his heart, leans not on his own understanding, acknowledges Him in all his ways, and is content that 'he shall direct thy paths' (Prov. 3:5-6) — without demanding a wet fleece on dry ground to do it.
roots_summary: Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40) was unbelief graciously accommodated, not a method to copy; God guides by His Word (Ps. 119:105), wisdom, and providence (Prov. 16:9), not by signs we devise — for sign-seeking is rebuked (Matt. 12:39; 4:7).
roots_lines: English: an idiom from Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40), wrongly taken as a guidance method to imitate.
The narrative's point: Gideon asked more proof of a promise already given (Judg. 6:16) and feared presumption (6:39) — God's patience, not Gideon's method.
God's appointed guidance: Ps. 119:105 (the Word), Prov. 11:14 (counsel), Prov. 16:9 (providence) — not signs demanded; sign-seeking is rebuked (Matt. 12:39).
usage: He 'put out a fleece' and waited for a sign, but Gideon's fleece was fear God indulged, not faith God commended.
Refusing to act until an arbitrary token appears is not trusting God; it edges toward 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.'
God guides by His Word, by counsel, and by providence — not by wet fleece on dry ground that we demand of Him.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Gideon's fleece was unbelief graciously accommodated, not a guidance method; God guides by His Word and providence, not by signs we demand.
